pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Find 1000 more or less than a number by recognising that only the thousands digit changes (4,562 → 5,562 / 3,562), extending the 10-more/100-more pattern to the next place — unless a boundary forces a roll-over (9,500 + 1000 = 10,500).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): count in multiples and find 1000 more or less than a given number (place-value fluency).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): generalises 2.NBT.8 (±10/±100) into the thousands place; 4.NBT.1 place-value relationships.
• Operational details — Use a place-value chart / Gattegno chart so +1000 steps the thousands digit while others hold; connect to counting in 1000s on a number line. Contrast +10, +100, +1000 side by side so the child tracks which column responds. Teach the roll-over boundary explicitly. Demand the 'which digit changes' reasoning.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): finds 1000 more/less with no boundary, using a chart. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): does it mentally, naming the thousands digit as the one that changes. Tier C (age 9, extending): handles roll-overs (9,500+1000) and generalises to numbers beyond 10,000.
bestPractices: Extend the established pattern: +1000 steps the thousands digit, others unchanged — keep asking 'which digit?'.
Contrast +10 / +100 / +1000 side by side so the child locates the responding column.
Use a Gattegno / place-value chart so one digit visibly changes per operation.
Teach roll-over boundaries (9,500 + 1000) as the interesting case.
Insist on place-value reasoning, not counting on, and generalise beyond 10,000.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten thousand-cubes for the concrete move
commonMisconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (stepping hundreds instead of thousands).
Counting on in smaller steps instead of jumping the place.
Assuming only one digit ever changes, mishandling roll-over.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: find 1000 more or less than a four-digit number by recognising that normally only the thousands digit changes (4,562 → 5,562 or 3,562), extending the earlier +10/+100 pattern into the next place. The key exceptions are boundary crossings: adding 1000 when the thousands digit is 9 regroups into the ten-thousands place (9,500 + 1000 = 10,500), and subtracting 1000 can remove or reduce a higher digit (1,562 − 1000 = 562; 10,500 − 1000 = 9,500). Learners should justify which digit changes, not count on in smaller steps, and generalise beyond 10,000, where crossings such as 19,500 + 1000 = 20,500 change the ten-thousands digit too.

activities.title: Digit-stepper: which column responds to +1000?
feedback: If the learner expects the hundreds or ones to change, show only the thousands digit ticking and ask them to re-state which column a thousand lives in.
If they confuse 1000 more with 100 more (e.g. answer 4,662), run +100 and +1000 side by side so the differing columns are visible.
Reinforce correct predictions by having the learner say the thousands digit aloud before and after the press.
activities.rationale: Acting on the number and watching a single column respond makes 'which digit changes' concrete and self-correcting; side-by-side comparison with +10/+100 locates the responding column. An interactive stepper is one effective medium, but a place-value chart with counters or a labelled number line can carry the same comparison.
sourceClaims: Mentally adding/subtracting a power of ten changing a single place generalises the Grade 2 ±10/±100 standard.
learnerActions: Start from a four-digit number such as 4,562 shown in a place-value chart or on a number line.
Press +1000 (and −1000) and observe which digit moves: the thousands digit ticks 4→5 for +1000 (giving 5,562) or 4→3 for −1000 (giving 3,562) while hundreds, tens and ones stay locked.
Before each press, predict the result and name the digit that will change; then check against what moves.
Compare +10, +100 and +1000 side by side on the same starting number, saying which column each operation drives.
Use a 0–10,000 number-line view to see ±1000 as equal hops along the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding or subtracting 1000 normally changes only the thousands digit, extending the same place-value logic that governs +10 and +100.

activities.title: The roll-over: when a place fills up
feedback: If the answer is 0,300 or stays 9,300, point out that the thousand must be carried; walk through 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands = 10,300.
If the answer is 19,300, check that they added exactly one thousand, not ten thousand.
Treat the boundary as a short targeted rehearsal of the single roll, not a re-teach of the whole idea.
activities.rationale: Boundary cases are where place-value reasoning is genuinely tested, so making the carry explicit addresses the common 9,000s/10,000-crossing error directly.
sourceClaims: Boundary roll-overs are the key teaching case for more/less across places.
learnerActions: Start from a boundary number such as 9,500 or 9,300.
Press +1000 and watch the thousands digit pass 9: it rolls 9→0 while a carry moves left, opening a new ten-thousands column (9,500 → 10,500; 9,300 → 10,300).
State in words why the number gains a digit: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands.
Rehearse just the single roll in reasoning: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands, so 9,300 + 1000 = 10,300 — not 0,300, not 9,300, not 19,300.
Try numbers beyond 10,000 to confirm the same place-value rule continues, including crossings such as 19,500 + 1000 = 20,500 and 10,500 − 1000 = 9,500.
activities.intendedInsight: When the thousands digit passes 9, the 'only one digit changes' pattern has a principled exception: the place fills up and regroups into the ten-thousands place (opening a new place for 9,500 → 10,500, or raising an existing ten-thousands digit for 19,500 → 20,500); the reverse crossing happens when subtracting (10,500 − 1000 = 9,500).

activities.title: Scored fluency and boundary checks
feedback: For a plain-case slip, ask which single digit should have moved.
For a boundary slip, redirect to the single-roll rehearsal (9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands).
Note: scored practice confirms fluency but does not by itself build the conceptual 'which digit' reasoning — pair it with the stepper/chart activities.
activities.rationale: Mixed plain and boundary items discriminate between a learner who only handles the easy case and one who regroups correctly across the thousands boundary.
learnerActions: Answer fill-in items such as '1000 more than 4,562 = __' and '1000 less than 4,562 = __'.
Answer which-digit-changes questions for ordinary cases.
Tackle boundary items deliberately, e.g. 9,500 + 1000 and 9,300 + 1000, writing the full regrouped answer.
Use a slider on a 0–10,000 line to land exactly 1000 away from a given point.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure, quick retrieval of 1000 more/less, including the regrouping boundary, confirms the place-value reasoning is fluent.

constraints: Demand place-value reasoning ('which digit changes, and why') rather than counting on in 1000s.
A static annotated chart is a useful reference but does not let the learner perform the transformation; pair any static image with an action (counters, stepper, or spoken prediction).

Recognition-only items (multiple choice 'which digit changes?') confirm identification but do not elicit independent construction of the answer; include fill-in and boundary items that require producing the regrouped number.
Scored quizzes assess and rehearse fluency; they do not substitute for the comparison work that builds the underlying concept.
Teach the roll-over boundary explicitly as the key case, and generalise to numbers beyond 10,000.
Timed/fluency modes are optional for securing speed, not a prerequisite for understanding.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Of the three cited sources, only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified; the CCSS generalisation and the NCETM 'boundary roll-overs are the key teaching case' claims are marked unverified in the source row. Treat the 'key teaching case' framing as a pedagogical emphasis, not an established comparative-efficacy finding.
Arithmetic check: 4,562 + 1000 = 5,562; 4,562 − 1000 = 3,562; 9,500 + 1000 = 10,500; 9,300 + 1000 = 10,300 — all confirmed correct as stated in the source.

The DfE claim establishes the curriculum skill/topic and underpins the overall objective, but it was removed from activity[0].sourceClaims because that activity's rationale is about the action/comparison pedagogy, not the topic itself; only the CCSS ±10/±100 generalisation claim was retained there.

The source's 'possible' interactive-image and 'poor' conversation/3D ratings were catalog fit judgements; retained only as the scaffold-limit note that static images need an accompanying action, without asserting any medium universally cannot teach this skill.
Activity 3's rationale (mixed items discriminate between learners) is inherited assessment-design reasoning; no source claim directly supports it, so its sourceClaims list is empty.

probeDeeper: Which digit changes when you find 1000 more? Does any other digit move?
9,300 + 1000 — does it become a five-digit number? Why?
1000 less than 4,562 — did the hundreds/tens/ones change at all?
assess.correctAnswer: 5,562; 3,562; 10,300 — changing only the thousands digit, and rolling into a new place when it passes 9.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adjusts the wrong place — changes the hundreds (or another digit) instead of the thousands
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the thousands column; add one thousand-block and watch only that column change (unless it overflows).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 1000 more than 4,562 comes out as 4,662 or 4,563.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to roll into a new place: 9,300 + 1000 → 0,300 or stays 9,300 or gives 19,300
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole idea — rehearse the single roll: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands = 10,300.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The boundary case is malformed or not carried to ten-thousands.

responseLevels.gap: Adjusts the wrong place or cannot cross the thousands boundary.
responseLevels.full: Finds 1000 more/less for any number, changing only the thousands digit and regrouping into a new place when needed.
responseLevels.partial: Handles the plain case but stumbles when the thousands digit rolls past 9.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask quickly and watch the method: '1000 more than 4,562? ... 1000 less than 4,562? ... 1000 more than 9,300?' The last one crosses into the ten-thousands — watch what happens.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 4,562 checks the plain case (only the thousands digit moves); 9,300 + 1000 forces a roll from 9 thousands into ten-thousands, exposing whether the child regroups or malforms the number. Watching the working shows which digit they touch.
